The analysis dashboard

Source: vignettes/dashboard.Rmd
dashboard.Rmd

rmblapp() opens a dashboard over the package’s analyses in your browser. It runs on your machine, in your R session. It needs the shiny package.

rmblapp()                          # start empty, load data at the left
rmblapp(indiex("health"))          # start with a data frame
rmblapp(capsule = "path/to/capsule")

From a terminal, rmbl app [PATH] [--port N] [--no-browser] does the same. PATH is a CSV file or a capsule directory.

Every analysis shows the R call it ran, and it runs exactly that call. Copy the call into a script and you get the same result. When a function refuses, the tab shows the refusal in the package’s words, with explerr()’s note on where it comes from.

Loading data

The panel at the left takes a CSV file (plain or gzip), a capsule directory, or a table from data.rmorie.com. For a capsule it loads the pinned data file. For data.rmorie.com, sign in first with rmbl login. The app never holds your data key: dload() reads it from where rmbl login stored it. The column types are listed under the source. Each tab also offers example data, so you can try every form before loading your own.

The tabs

  • Describe: profcols(), freqtbl(), cortbl(), mahaoutl() and missgrid(), plus ridgelines, distribution functions, violins, hexagonal bins and concentration curves.
  • Year over year: yoy() with the period, value, groups, the smallest base for a percentage and which direction is better. Download the result as the yoyhtml() page.
  • Rates: rtcalc(), ratechg() and shrs(). A rate per population and a share of a total stay apart.
  • Trends: trndtst() (Mann-Kendall with the Theil-Sen slope), stepchg(), cnttrnd(), a calendar heatmap, a horizon chart, small multiples and a bump chart.
  • Survey: svydes() with weights, strata, clusters or replicate weights, then svyest() or svycmp().
  • Distributions: dstfit() fits candidate distributions and ranks them, with density, QQ, PP and tail plots. You can draw a synthetic sample from the best fit with mksyncol().
  • Drift: the drift app, when this version has it.
  • Capsule: a capsule’s provenance, manifest, attestation and bundle files. Its buttons run vrfcps() and cpschk(), or cpsrfrsh().
  • Policy: the panel designs on unit-by-period data, from plndid() and evstudy() to syndid(), wcb(), plnpwr() and tse(). The panel names the assumption they share: without the policy, the outcomes would have moved in parallel. Read the pre-period coefficients and the cohort trends before the estimate.
  • First Nations, Métis and Inuit: Statistics Canada’s tables as indiex() ships them, or your own in the same layout. Each distinction is reported on its own. Suppressed cells stay suppressed, and the quality flags are shown. The panel states the OCAP® and CARE principles and links the source tables.
  • Courts and corrections: stkflow(), caseflow(), clrdcmp(), dispmix(), lifetbl(), crmdens(), knoxtst(), rgnmapintg(), and the SIU readers siuprs() and siuso() on pasted text.
  • Air pollution: a plume map (plmfld()), a downwind profile and receptor concentrations (gplume()), the concentration-response functions, polbrdn() and vrfpol().
  • Hawkes: chwkfit() with plothwk() (intensity, time-rescaling check, branching tree) and chwksim().
  • Proof ledger: a ledger from a file, a capsule or an installed package, its theorems and ldgrchk()’s rows.
  • Report: what you added from the tabs. Save it as one HTML page with the plots as inline SVG, as Markdown, or copy it as a GitHub comment.
  • Settings: the theme (light, dark or as the system is set), printed digits, and the seed the seeded analyses use.

The same work in a script

What the Distributions tab runs:

set.seed(1)
wait <- stats::rgamma(300, 2, 0.5)
fit <- dstfit(wait, nboot = 50)
fit$table[, c("rank", "family", "aic", "ks")]
#>   rank      family      aic         ks
#> 1    1     weibull 1351.093 0.02543328
#> 2    2       gamma 1352.651 0.03906373
#> 3    3   lognormal 1387.446 0.07363527
#> 4    4 exponential 1420.742 0.14763458
#> 5    5           t 1428.453 0.08260813
#> 6    6      normal 1438.345 0.09559638
#> 7    7      pareto 1895.463 0.36065534
plot(fit, which = "qq", fams = c("gamma", "weibull"))

And what the Proof ledger tab runs on the sample ledger:

led <- ldgrread(system.file("extdata", "ledger_sample.json", package = "rmoriebricklayer"))
led
#> Proof ledger rmoriebricklayer sample ledger: 3 theorems (1 proved, 1 sorry, 1 axiom)
#>   https://github.com/rootcoder007/rmorie-proofs @ 0123456789ab, Lean v4.12.0
ldgrchk(led)[, c("check", "ok", "severity")]
#>                                                check    ok severity
#> 1                                 proved: gini-equal  TRUE    error
#> 2     covered: gini-equal rmoriebricklayer::ginicoef  TRUE    error
#> 3                                  check: gini-equal  TRUE    error
#> 4                            proved: lorenz-monotone FALSE    error
#> 5 covered: lorenz-monotone rmoriebricklayer::lorenzc  TRUE    error
#> 6                                proved: float-round FALSE     warn

A ledger records the theorems of a formal-proof build and the functions each one covers. Any package can ship one in inst/ledger/, and the tab finds it there. A theorem counts as proved only when no sorry remains. An axiom is assumed, not proved, so it shows as a warning. A ledger pinned in a capsule (provenance kind: "ledger") is checked by rmbl verify too.
